name: Effect size
seoDesc: Effect size: work out experimental sample mean from the control sample mean and the experimental standard deviation. A free statistics calculator with the…
summary: Give the Effect size calculator the control sample mean, the experimental standard deviation, the pooled standard deviation and the correlation coefficient and it returns experimental sample mean. That makes it useful for an assignment, a report or a data discussion where you need a defensible number. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Effect size calculator work?
sections.html:
The Effect size calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports experimental sample mean in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the control sample mean, the experimental standard deviation, the pooled standard deviation and the correlation coefficient.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Effect size calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Experimental sample mean=control sample mean − effect size × pooled standard deviation
Control standard deviation=the square root of (-(experimental standard deviation ^ 2) + 2 × (pooled standard deviation ^ 2))
Effect size=2 × correlation coefficient × the square root of (-1 ÷ ((correlation coefficient ^ 2) − 1))
Variance=the absolute value of ((correlation coefficient ^ 2))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Control sample mean = 10, Pooled standard deviation = 10 and Effect size = 10. Working through the relationship above gives Experimental sample mean = -90, Correlation coefficient = 0.9806 and Variance = 0.9615.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Experimental sample mean = -90, Correlation coefficient = 0.9806 and Variance = 0.9615 should be roughly the size you expected from Control sample mean = 10 and Pooled standard deviation = 10.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Effect size calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a result a piece of software produced
  • Turning raw numbers into something you can quote
  • Deciding how much confidence a sample really supports
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the control sample mean, the experimental standard deviation and the pooled standard deviation — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Effect size calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

faq.q: What does the Effect size calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns experimental sample mean, derived from the control sample mean, the experimental standard deviation and the pooled standard deviation. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Effect size calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the control sample mean, the experimental standard deviation, the pooled standard deviation and the correlation coefficient, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Experimental sample mean = -90. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Effect size calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
